chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majilawayh narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to me from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Suleiman al-Basri, from Dawud al-Raqqi, from al-Rayyan [Rabab], his wife, who said:

I prepared a sweet dish (khabeeص) and brought it to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He was eating it, so I placed the sweet dish before him. He was feeding it to his companions, and I heard him say: 'Whoever feeds a believer a morsel of sweetness, Allah will turn away bitterness from him on the Day of Resurrection.'

key_terms.خَبِیص: A sweet dish made from dates and flour, a common pre-Islamic and early Islamic food.
key_terms.مَرَارَه: Bitterness (often referring to the hardships or bitterness of the Day of Judgment).

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for feeding a believer something sweet?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-Amal* highlights the spiritual merit of *tabarruj* (showing affection) through food, specifically sweets, within the Shia tradition of honoring the Ahl al-Bayt and their companions. By feeding Imam al-Sadiq, who then shared it with his companions, Rabab al-Raqqi exemplifies the chain of merit where a simple act of generosity transforms into divine relief from the 'bitterness' of accountability on the Day of Resurrection.

en.sayed-athar-husain-rizvi-&-sayed-maqs: 1.  Dawood  Raqqi  narrates  that  his  wife  Rabab  said:

I prepared a sweet dish of dates and took it to Imam Ja’far Sadiq  (a.s.).  He  ate  it  himself  as  well  as  offered  it  to  his companions. She heard him say, “One who offers a morsel of sweet to a believer, Allah will keep the bitterness of the Day of Judgment away from him.”
